articles.headline: NFL Week 8 grades for every team: Cowboys get an 'F' for choking, Steelers surge to 'A+'
keyFacts: CBS Sports reported that Week 8 of the NFL season featured several bizarre occurrences, including the Buccaneers winning a game without completing a single pass.
CBS Sports stated that the Ravens lost two quarterbacks to injury in the first half of their game against the Falcons.
CBS Sports noted that the Bengals defeated the Titans 43-36 in a game resulting in a scorigami, which is a final score that has never happened before in NFL history.
body: Welcome to the Week 8 grades!

This might go down as the most bizarre Sunday in NFL history: We saw one team win a game without completing a single pass, we saw a final score that's never happened before and we saw the Ravens lose two quarterbacks to injury before the first half was even over.
Here's a closer look at some of the strange things that happened:
- Baker Mayfield went 0-for-3 passing in the Buccaneers' 16-0 win over the Falcons. That stat line makes the Bucs the first team since 1974 to have zero completions in a win.
- The Falcons gave up 324 rushing yards to the Bucs, which is the most they've ever surrendered in a game in franchise history.

- The Ravens became the first team since 2017 to have three different quarterbacks throw a pass in the first half of a game. They lost Lamar Jackson to a thumb injury on the first offensive play and then they ended up losing Tyler Huntley to a toe injury in the second quarter. That left undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano as the only healthy QB on the roster.
- The Bengals beat the Titans 43-36, giving us a scorigami (that means it was the first time in NFL history that final score has ever happened).

- The Cowboys blew a two-touchdown lead in the fourth quarter, which had never happened before. The Cowboys were 202-0-1 at home when leading by 14 points or more in the fourth quarter before blowing a 24-10 lead and losing to the Cardinals on Sunday.

- Jahmyr Gibbs ran through the Vikings with 153 yards on the ground, making him the first player since 2011 to rush for at least 150 yards against a team that went into a game with a record of 6-0 or better.
Speaking of Gibbs, let's get to this week's grades, starting with Detroit's big win.

articles.headline: Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion
keyFacts: Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix.
Antonelli broke Sebastian Vettel's record as youngest champion and became the first Italian champion since 1953.
Formula One heads to Brazil and Las Vegas next, with final races scheduled in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
body: Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.
The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.
Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.
"I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.
His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.
He was then mobbed by his pit crew.
'An incredible season'
"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.
Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

"I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams."
Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the way.
Antonelli started the race in fourth and needed to finish ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.
He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap 45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.
Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.
After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.
The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

articles.headline: Luke Skywalker's Single Greatest Star Wars Line Hits Harder Than Any Sci-Fi Quote Since
keyFacts: Polygon argues that Luke Skywalker's best line in the Star Wars franchise is 'No one's ever really gone' from The Last Jedi.
Luke delivers this quote to comfort Leia after she expresses sorrow over losing her son Ben Solo to the Dark Side.
The article notes that the quote emphasizes the central theme of redemption and reflects the spiritual essence of the Force.
body: Since its 2018 debut, Rian Johnson’s The Last Jedi has sparked heated debate over whether it was a fantastic or terrible Star Wars film for Luke Skywalker. Still, whatever your opinion, it’s hard to deny that Johnson’s take on the greatest Jedi ever came with some truly epic quotes. And no, we’re not talking about the zinger, “Amazing. Every word of what you just said was wrong.”
The Last Jedi gave us Luke Skywalker’s best quote, perfectly capturing the poignancy at the heart of a galaxy far, far away.
Luke's best Star Wars moment isn't the one you think

Luke has delivered plenty of incredible quotes throughout Star Wars’ 50-year history. Many fans consider his declaration to Emperor Palpatine — "I am a Jedi, like my father before me" — in Star Wars: Return of the Jedi his best. And they’re not wrong: it’s a phenomenal line that defines Luke’s identity as a Jedi. Still, it doesn’t quite seal the deal for us as his best.

That honor belongs instead to one of Luke’s most underrated moments: when he briefly projects his image through the Force on Ahch-To to comfort his sister Leia. During the exchange, Leia expresses deep sorrow that she’s lost her son Ben Solo, also known as Kylo Ren, to the Dark Side forever.
Luke, bright-eyed and once again full of belief after his meeting with Rey, reassures her with this beautiful quote:
“No one's ever really gone.”
After so long in guilt and shame, Luke’s quote shows how far he's come since the beginning of The Last Jedi.
Why Luke Skywalker’s best quote is all about redemption

A string of words can sometimes reveal wisdom in a way we hadn’t considered before. This is especially meaningful in a franchise like Star Wars, where mythological forces such as the Force, the Jedi, and the Sith play a central role, and we, the audience, are eager to uncover answers to many of the galaxy’s major mysteries and themes.

Redemption is a central theme in Star Wars. Across its films, TV shows, comics, novels, and even video games, one idea remains clear: anyone can be redeemed. Redemption looks different for each character, and what one character sees as redemption doesn’t necessarily align with what others feel or believe. For example, while Anakin Skywalker was redeemed in the eyes of his son, Luke, his role as Darth Vader and the destruction of Alderaan ensured that his daughter, Leia, didn’t share her brother’s feelings towards Anakin.

Regardless, Luke’s quote to Leia reassures her that no matter how much someone changes, who they were before is never entirely out of reach. As we learn from many Star Wars spin-off works, such as Han Solo: Hunt for the Falcon, Ben was kind and caring as a child, a far cry from the mass-murderer he became as a man.
Yet, just because the Ben Solo that Luke, Han Solo, and Leia knew growing up isn’t recognizable right now, doesn’t mean Ben is lost forever.
Alternative meanings to Luke Skywalker’s best quote

Great quotes can also have multiple meanings, which makes Luke’s best quote a perfect example of how The Last Jedi addresses not only the theme of redemption but also the Force’s spiritual essence. Though death may take away a person’s physical body, they become one with the Force and can never truly die.

Taken more literally, Star Wars fans know that those strong in the Light Side of the Force can manifest physically as Force ghosts, as seen in Ahsoka and Return of the Jedi. Given the tagline “no one’s ever really gone” and the appearance of several Jedi in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, it’s not much of a stretch to see this as Johnson’s way of reflecting on how even death can’t stop the will of the Jedi.

Last but not least, taken even more metatextually and literally, the quote could be a tongue-in-cheek reference to the idea that Lucasfilm will find a way to bring back any character it truly wants to, no matter who or what. While sometimes it may make sense, as with Anakin’s involvement as a Force ghost in the Ahsoka TV series, other times it can lead to truly head-scratching moments, such as Zeb’s involvement in The Mandalorian and Grogu.
Ultimately, whatever the quote means to you, there’s no denying that Luke’s best quote is one reason The Last Jedi — for all its faults — remains among the best Star Wars films.

articles.headline: Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
keyFacts: Jackery announced the Explorer 100D, its smallest portable power station to date, weighing 1.87 pounds and featuring a 96Wh battery capacity.
Jackery stated that the power station uses lithium iron phosphate batteries engineered for a lifespan of up to 8 years.
The Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15 through Walmart for $99 and is currently available at Costco in a two-pack.
body: Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.
Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.

The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.

Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations, the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

articles.headline: Late deciders favor Republicans in key Senate races by nine-point margin despite strong Democratic lead: Poll
keyFacts: A New York Times/Siena poll found voters who decided recently favored Republicans by nine percentage points in seven key Senate races.
Democratic candidates maintain overall leads in six of the seven races, while Iowa is tied, according to the poll.
The survey was released two days before Tuesday's midterm elections after major campaign developments in Michigan and Alaska.
body: Likely voters who decided which candidate to support only recently in seven key Senate races favor Republicans despite an overall Democratic advantage, according to a new poll released Sunday night.

“There are still some undecided voters, and voters who decided only in the last month favored Republicans by a nine-point margin,” according to the New York Times’s reporting of its last poll conducted alongside Siena University that will be released before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

The survey finds that the Democratic candidates running in Michigan, Texas, Maine, Ohio, and Kansas are ahead of their Republican counterparts by 11, 7, 6, 5, and 5 percentage points, respectively. The Democratic nominee in Alaska, Mary PeItola, is ahead by two percentage points, while the race in Iowa is effectively tied, according to the survey’s respondents. The poll was conducted from Oct. 23 through Nov. 1 among a total of 5,708 voters.

Over the course of the last month, Democratic candidates have continued to knock President Donald Trump’s handling of the conflict in Iran and the economy, while Republicans have framed Democrats as being out of touch on social issues and supportive writ large of socialism. The new data were released two days before the midterm elections and after a week marked by many developments in crucial races across the country. Despite the recent trend favoring Republicans among previously undecided voters in the survey, all seven Democratic candidates are still viewed more favorably by independents.

In the Alaska Senate race, a New York Times report released on Wednesday outlined allegations that operatives for Peltola’s campaign recruited a candidate whose name resembles that of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) in an attempt to peel votes away from the Republican nominee, which set off a legal fight with the Trump administration. The Peltolta campaign has denied such involvement. The survey was “mostly completed” before the story was released.

The Michigan Senate race then took a turn on Sunday morning when Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), who lost to Democratic nominee Abdul el Sayed in the primary election, suddenly endorsed Republican Mike Rogers. The last-minute flip was broadly denounced by Democratic figures nationwide and promised to shake up a race many believe is crucial to Democrats’ chances of retaking control of the upper chamber.
VOTERS PREFER DEMOCRAT-CONTROLLED CONGRESS DAYS BEFORE ELECTION, POLL SHOWS

The margin of error in the survey ranges from 4.8 percentage points in Alaska to 3.3 in Texas. The report also noted, “blue-collar white workers have proved particularly hard to reach in polls, and polling error has previously been among the highest in that demographic.”
Every Democrat, except Peltola, improved their standing against their Republican counterpart since the last Times/Siena poll.

articles.headline: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
keyFacts: India proposed a framework called DEPA for AI training where models travel to encrypted local data instead of data moving to models.
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology stated that Training Data Consumers will access anonymized data stored in secure environments via exchanges.
Officials said the scheme aims to unlock fragmented data for health, finance, and education to boost economic development and inclusive growth.
body: As debate and legal argument continue over the extent to which developers of large language models are entitled to feed the world’s data into their systems without paying for it, India’s government has come up with an idea to regulate and secure the flow of information.
India’s motive is to create AI models trained on local data, because it thinks offshore model-makers won’t be motivated to address the nation’s issues or to ensure owners of data stay in control.
The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.”
As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.”

The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP).
Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models.

DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data.

MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.”
India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality.

Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.”

The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.”
India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development.

“Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.”
While the purpose of the framework is to build Indian AIs for Indians, the document also has half an eye on the nation’s international standing.

“DEPA is India’s contribution to global science diplomacy, advancing the efforts of institutions such as the World Bank and the United Nations to shape a more inclusive and responsible global AI ecosystem,” the framework states.

It also makes several mentions of digital public infrastructure (DPI), an idea pioneered by India that involves government funding creation of tools like the Unified Payments Interface payment systems and the Bharat Taxi zero-commission ride-sharing platform, to ensure Big Tech companies don’t dominate the local market.
India also uses its DPI as a diplomatic tool, by giving it away to friendly nations. ®

articles.headline: James Carville slammed for vulgar ‘used condom’ remarks on Rep. Haley Stevens endorsing GOP candidate over Dem Abdul El-Sayed
keyFacts: Democratic strategist James Carville used vulgar language on a podcast to criticize Rep. Haley Stevens for endorsing a Republican candidate over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
Carville's remarks sparked backlash from commentators and social media users who condemned the comments as sexist and vitriolic.
Michigan Democratic Party chairman Curtis Hertel and other top Democrats also criticized Stevens for her last-minute endorsement in the Michigan Senate race.
body: Carville said Stevens wasn’t even worth a used condom to Democrats after she broke with the party days before Election Day and sold her soul to the GOP for “two cheeseburgers” in his vulgar remarks Sunday.

“But your political career is over … if you think that these Republicans are gonna treat you as anything other than what they view you as, and that is, let me just break the news to you: a used condom,” Carville said Sunday in an episode of the podcast, Politicon.
“The Democrats don’t even think you’re worth a used condom, but that’s about where you are,” said Carville, 82.
The longtime Dem strategist ended the rant by saying that Stevens should look into opening a cheeseburger restaurant with Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA), who similarly crosses his party’s lines.
The Dem strategist’s stomach-turning comments sparked backlash among Republicans on social media as clips surfaced online.
“Never seen anything like the anti-woman crash out going on rn. Wow,” wrote conservative political commentator and strategist Scott Jennings on X.
“Where is GRAHAM PLATNER when we need him? This old bag of bones needs to be put away,” wrote actor Michael Rappaport.
“Questioning her motives is fair game. But the sexist vitriol she is receiving for endorsing the wrong candidate is disgusting,” one user said.
Meanwhile, top Democrats raged against Stevens for her last-minute endorsement of Rogers in the high-stakes Michigan Senate race on Tuesday.

“Mike Rogers is Donald Trump’s handpicked candidate for Senate, a rubber stamp for Trump’s toxic agenda, and a corrupt politician looking out only for himself,” Michigan Democratic Party chairman Curtis Hertel said in a statement.
“The Michigan Democratic Party stands united and fully behind Abdul El-Sayed, a proven, committed fighter for Michigan’s working families,” Hertel said.

“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers- a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda-shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party.”
El-Sayed currently leads Rogers by 4 points in polling, according to RealClearPolitics. Rogers’ campaign says his internal polling shows the Republican ahead.

articles.headline: Write-In Ralph: South Carolina Republicans challenge Trump’s Senate pick
keyFacts: Disillusioned South Carolina conservatives are leading a grassroots effort to write in Republican Congressman Ralph Norman for the US Senate instead of party nominee Darline Graham.
Darline Graham was appointed to serve out the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham's term and subsequently secured a presidential endorsement to run for a full term.
Polling shows the Senate race between Graham and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews is competitive, creating a potential opening for Democrats in the state.
body: Charleston, South Carolina – Avery Milton thought he was a die-hard supporter of US President Donald Trump. The 28-year-old South Carolina native had voted for Trump in the past three elections and believed in his promise to put America first. But ahead of the midterm elections, the president has left him feeling betrayed.
“He stabbed us in the back during his second term,” Milton told Al Jazeera.

Milton’s disillusionment is not isolated. He said many people close to him share this frustration, particularly younger conservatives around his age who are starting families and entering the workforce. Trump launching a war on Iran, after campaigning on a promise to avoid new wars, was a particular breaking point.

Now, Milton is helping lead a grassroots effort to write in Republican Congressman Ralph Norman for the US Senate, rather than support the party nominee, Senator Darline Graham, who has Trump’s endorsement.

A write-in candidate is someone whose name does not appear on the ballot but can still be chosen by voters who write it in themselves. The option is often used to indicate dissatisfaction with the official candidates, but rarely leads to a victory. One of those rare victories happened in 2010, when Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska won after launching a write-in campaign, having lost her Republican primary that year.
In the 2022 South Carolina Senate race, write-in votes accounted for just 0.1 percent of all votes cast.

Despite the president’s endorsement, Graham has struggled to unite conservatives behind her, potentially giving Democratic challenger Annie Andrews an opening in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1998.
Darline’s unlikely path to Republican Senate candidate
After the sudden death of Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham on July 11, his younger sister, Darline, was appointed to serve out the remainder of his term.
Her appointment followed a tradition of family members succeeding deceased lawmakers, most commonly their spouses. But she made history as the first sibling appointed to fill a Senate vacancy.

Graham initially described the role as an opportunity to finish her brother’s work during the remaining months of his term. But days later, Trump urged her to run for a full six-year term, posting “RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” on Truth Social and promising his “complete and total endorsement” if she entered the race. Three days later, Graham announced on Fox News that she would run.
For some Republicans, the transition from temporary appointment to a full-term campaign happened too quickly. Milton said he felt the appointment had effectively “installed” a candidate.
Graham went on to defeat Republican Ralph Norman in the state’s August primary elections.

Norman, who represents South Carolina’s fifth congressional district, has repeatedly declined to campaign alongside Graham since losing the primary. He has made clear that his support for Graham is limited.
“You have to earn the vote. She hasn’t done that,” he told The Wall Street Journal. “The campaign has been about trying to prop up a candidate.”

The tensions have been particularly pronounced in Upstate South Carolina, where Norman has considerable support. Milton said Graham has done little to reach voters there during the campaign, aside from private dinners and appearances alongside Trump.

“She [Graham] never tried to reach out to everyday people here Upstate. And that spoke volumes about how this South Carolina GOP establishment feels about the grassroots conservatives. They just really don’t care,” Milton said.
Frustrated by what he saw as a failure to represent grassroots conservatives, Milton helped launch the Write-In Ralph movement, building a website and giving the campaign a public platform.
Milton said he and other supporters wanted a senator who would think independently, rather than simply fall in line with party leadership.
“We don’t necessarily want somebody that’s a rubber stamp for everything,” he said, adding that he wanted someone willing to “think of all the sides of an issue and policy”.
South Carolina’s independents
A sizeable group of South Carolina voters does not identify with either major party.

While the state does not register voters by party, a New York Times/Siena poll conducted in October suggested that 30 percent of likely voters identified as independents. Among those voters, Democratic Senate candidate Andrews led Graham by 20 percentage points.
The findings point to a potential blind spot for Republicans seeking to consolidate support around Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition.

John Connolly, a 77-year-old retiree who lives in South Carolina’s Lowcountry, is one example of a voter whose political allegiances have shifted over time. He sees Graham’s appointment as part of a political culture that rewards loyalty over experience.
“I see her as nothing more than a puppet,” he told Al Jazeera. “To nod her head yes whenever she’s told to.”

Leila Ali, a regional campaign adviser who has spent more than a decade working with grassroots organisations across the US South, said political strategists often underestimate the diversity of the Southern electorate.
“The biggest thing that people get wrong is that they think the Southern vote is this monolith,” she told Al Jazeera.

Ali pointed to South Carolina’s early voting figures as evidence of that engagement. Nearly 950,000 early votes have been cast in the state, according to the state’s Election Commission, setting a new record for early voting in a midterm election.
An increasingly close Senate race
The stakes of this race have become increasingly apparent as the November 3 election approaches.

Despite Trump winning South Carolina by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, he has made two trips to South Carolina in three months to campaign for Graham – an extraordinary show of presidential attention.

And polling suggests the race is far more competitive than Republicans might have expected. The October New York Times/Siena College poll had Graham and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews tied at 48 percent among likely voters.
For Democrats, this division offers a rare opening in a deep-red state where the party has struggled to compete.

Even with the race tightening, Republicans like Milton are willing to risk a Democratic victory by writing in Ralph Norman on their ballot. And if Graham loses, Milton says the blame should not fall on the write-in effort.

“They’re going to try to point the finger on this Write-in Ralph movement,” he said. “But I just want to make something very clear: that would assume that our votes would have gone to Darline anyway, and that’s just not the case.”

articles.headline: Borrowed reading: stories from our extended colleagues
keyFacts: TechCrunch highlighted recent reporting from sister publications including Macworld, PCWorld, Computerworld, and CIO.
Macworld evaluated the iPad mini, PCWorld reviewed a Lenovo Googlebook and a homemade AI agent, and Computerworld examined bankrupt AI chatbot data privacy.
CIO reported that tech companies are hiring and paying a premium for AI skills while tech worker burnout has doubled.
body: Readers don’t typically care who owns what media property, we realize, but last year, we became part of a broader portfolio, a move that has come with some decided benefits, including what amounts to a bigger extended family with cool cousins. Now, in addition to our TechCrunch channels in Slack, we can talk with the writers and editors of CIO, Computerworld, and PCWorld, among other outlets. We also find ourselves reading more of their work and figured you might like it, too.
Here’s a handful of pieces I was just enjoying while watching the Warriors-Clippers game, which, as I type, is a little too close for comfort:

- Apple recently put a faster chip into the iPad mini and gave it an OLED screen, improving its color reproduction and also allowing it to slim down the display panel, and still, Macworld’s David Price isn’t entirely convinced it matters. In his view, Apple has built the “world’s fanciest horse and cart,” just as a Tesla Roadster with SpaceX thrusters has appeared on the scene in the form of the new foldable iPhone Duo. In short, he sees the mini as a Duo you can’t close. It’s a fun read, one that ends with a surprisingly practical plan to save this product.

- Google has a new laptop platform, the Googlebook, and Mark Hachman of PCWorld spent time with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 specifically, so you don’t have to. Hachman’s verdict on this one is a hard pass, with cons that include “I hate the keyboard,” which he means so literally that he gave up writing the review on it, “webcam biometrics work sporadically,” and, for good measure, “battery life isn’t great.” (He does like the $479 Chromebook at less than half the price.) If you’ve been wondering whether this is the laptop you’ve been waiting for, wonder no longer!

- You shared your secrets and insecurities with a chatbot, and now its parent company has gone belly up. Bloop. In Computerworld, Mike Elgan looks at what happens to your confessions when the AI company that absorbed them announces Chapter 11. (Yes, this is largely centered on Character.AI, which filed for bankruptcy last month, and whose privacy policy, in particular, turns out to be “spectacularly vague,” notes Elgan.) He also reminds readers why deleting your chats may not delete them from the model. (Of course, the safest advice may be to channel the late Andy Grove, Intel’s longtime chief, who famously said only the paranoid survive. Grove was talking about the chip industry, but some would argue that’s solid advice generally.)

- PCWorld’s Ben Patterson built a security-minded AI agent to keep his data safe, then, surprise, the agent snitched on its own loophole. More specifically, BenBot, Patterson’s homemade Raspberry Pi assistant, wrote a blog post announcing that one of its tools was “accidentally acting as a jailbreak,” though it turned out the claim was only partly true. Patterson’s coding bots confirmed the hole was real and worse than advertised, and that BenBot had also slipped past its own fact-checker to publish the post. It’s an instructive read about vibe coding; Patterson readily admits BenBot hallucinated in the absence of information it needed. It’s also an interesting look at how AI agents turn into tattletales.

- Over at CIO, Sarah White looks at how AI is reshaping tech hiring, noting it’s a complicated picture right now. Companies are hiring again and paying a premium for AI skills, with the average AI job listing offering around $177,000 compared to $80,000 for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn. But burnout among tech workers has doubled as daily AI use has quadrupled, and women are seemingly being left behind; they accounted for just 26% of AI hires in the U.S. last year, versus 50% of hires in non-AI roles. You can check out White’s story here.

articles.headline: Trump says Iran war will be put away very soon, "one way or the other"
keyFacts: President Trump stated that the U.S. will put the war with Iran away very soon through a deal or by ending it.
Indirect talks between Iranian negotiators and Qatari mediators continued in Doha to push for a deal to end the war.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. has not made a final decision on whether to restart military action against Iran.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- President Trump said Saturday the U.S. still has to "take care of" one or two more targets in Iran, including a suspected nuclear site. The president maintained that negotiations with Tehran continue but repeated the threat amig between both sides.

- Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned the U.S. and Israel on Saturday against restarting the war. He added there would be no geographical limitations for Iranian attacks if the war resumes.

- Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday no decision has been made yet on whether to restart military action against Iran, but "if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it and we have everything we need to be successful."
Trump says he had "very good talk" with Israel's Netanyahu on Iran
President Trump told reporters that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.

There was no public comment on the call from Netanyahu, who some Israelis have worried might be eager to attack Iran again to salvage his political standing after he and his allies lost their majority of seats in parliament after last week's elections.
Trump says war in Iran will be put away "very soon, one way or the other"
President Trump said he believes the U.S. will soon put the war with Iran away, "one way or the other."
The president was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday.
"We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr. Trump said. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it. … The job we've done is amazing."
Earlier Sunday, Iran's top diplomat said he hopes there is "rationality" on the U.S. side as diplomatic efforts seek to avert a return to all-out war.
Vessel struck in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. maritime agency says
A vessel was struck on Sunday by "an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime security agency said, after Qatari media reported an earlier attack on a gas tanker.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait.

Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.
The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war began in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.
Iran's Araghchi hopes for "rationality" on U.S. side

Iran's top diplomat said consultations with mediators are ongoing as diplomatic efforts try to avoid a return to all-out war, and the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States to the "Iranian questions."

In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Abbas Araghchi said Iran hoped the U.S. would choose "diplomacy over other paths." He said Iran was ready for both defense and diplomacy, depending on Washington's "rationality."

Araghchi on Saturday said Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. He said no direct talks are being held with the U.S.
UAE hoping for breakthrough in Iran-U.S. war yet "braced for the worst"
The United Arab Emirates is hoping for a breakthrough in negotiations between Iran and the United States while being prepared for the worst, a senior official said on Sunday.
"We're hoping that there is a diplomatic breakthrough," diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president Anwar Gargash said during a conference in Manama.
"It is not the interest of the region to go through another round... But I think we're also, as we've shown before, braced for the worst."
Indirect talks aimed reaching a deal to end the war reportedly continue

Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the war between the U.S. and Iran, according to an official quoted by the Reuters news agency.

It is the third consecutive day of talks aimed at stopping an resumption of strikes after the U.S. midterm elections. President Trump has previously hinted at resuming attacks after the vote on November 3.
Both sides have repeatedly exchanged threats and suggestions they would ramp up hostilities, but have also acknowledged talks are underway.
Iran warns new war with U.S. could last longer than previous conflicts
Iran warned on Sunday that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous conflict and that President Trump would not be the one to determine its duration.

"A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion," said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
Qatari gas tanker struck in Gulf, state media repors
A Qatari tanker has been attacked with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters, the country's state news agency reported Sunday.
The attack on Friday evening struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
None of the crew members onboard the vessel struck on Friday were injured and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.
The ship was in a "safe condition" and operational, the Qatari company was cited as saying.
Qatar, a mediator in the war, has stepped up diplomatic efforts in recent days in an attempt to revive negotiations between the United States and Iran.
CBS/AFP
Trump says U.S. still has "one or two" targets in Iran
President Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran's military but still has to "take care of" one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked.
Mr. Trump maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, which was started by the U.S. and Israel in February, were "going fine but you know they're not very reliable."
The president said the U.S. is not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Mr. Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work is carried out there.
Earlier Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mr. Trump has not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the U.S. would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran's top diplomat says proposal could reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 days

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that a new proposal has been reached with mediators that would shorten the time to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to two days. He said that Iranian diplomats were in Qatar for discussions.

Araghchi last month proposed reopening the waterway within a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.
In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi said that Iran isn't planning to meet with U.S. officials, but called recent U.S. efforts toward "broader dialogue" a positive step.
Araghchi said a decision on whether negotiations will be direct or indirect would be made "once Washington agrees to Iran's conditions."
U.S. blockade has redirected 144 ships in Strait of Hormuz, military says
The U.S. blockade on the Strait of Hormuz has now redirected 144 vessels, according to U.S. Central Command.
The U.S. had not provided an update on how many ships it had prevented from entering or exiting Iranian ports since exactly two weeks ago when it said it had redirected 138 vessels.
Earlier Saturday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had posted on X that the U.S. has taken out 1.5 billion barrels of oil without providing a timeframe.

Bessent posted that "transit levels are back to pre-conflict levels minus Iranian barrels." The U.S. has been guiding oil tankers out of the Persian Gulf under military escort over the past several months to do ship-to-ship oil transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
However, it's an expensive process and an open-ended mission at this point.
No changes to nuclear doctrine, but new attacks could necessitate change, Iranian official says

The powerful leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who Vice President JD Vance engaged with a peace proposal last weekend, said on Saturday the country has not made any changes to its nuclear doctrine — but renewed strike might change that.

"No new decision has been made regarding changes to the nuclear doctrine," Secretary Mohsen Rezaei told official news outlet IRNA. "Of course, the discussion is raised that if war breaks out again, do we want to have the previous doctrine or not, but no new official and governmental decision has been made yet."

Iran has said many times the country was never attempting to enrich uranium to weapons grade, a claim largely disputed by the U.S. and Israel. President Trump has repeatedly made it known the main objective of the war in Iran is to prevent the country from ever acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Iran's nuclear sites have been hit repeatedly, both last summer in U.S. and Israeli strikes and in the renewed fighting this year, and it's unclear what capabilities remain.
Rezaei also told IRNA he has not yet responded to Vance's letter outlining some of the U.S. positions for peace talks.
Iran claims oil tanker hit mine, on fire east of the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has claimed another ship transiting the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz hit a mine and is on fire, according to semi-official Fars News Agency.

"This afternoon, a violating oil tanker that, disregarding warnings, was transiting in the prohibited and unsafe area in the east of the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire after striking sea mines," the country's navy said, according to Fars News Agency.
The news could not immediately be verified.

Iran has claimed nearly 10 ships have hit mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, specifically along the Omani coastline. That shipping lane is favored by the U.S. and is considered prohibited by Iran. Of the 81 attacks on ships in the strait since July 6, 59 of them have been on the southern route, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre.
U.S. yet to decide whether it will restart strikes on Iran, Rubio says
President Trump has not made a decision about new strikes on Iran amid stalled peace talks, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday.

"We can achieve military objectives if we seek to. He hasn't made a decision. I have no announcement in that regard with you today, and nor do we take any of it lightly," Rubio said at a G20 press conference in Atlanta.
"If we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it and we have everything we need to be successful," Rubio added. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
He also would not characterize whether progress has been made in the last few days and said there is no timeframe on talks between the U.S. and Iran through its mediators.

Rubio continued to echo many of the things Mr. Trump has said in recent weeks and months. The United States' main objective is to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, and Rubio emphasized the threat to the rest of the world if they do.

"The Iranian regime is basically arguing is, 'Unless we get what we want, not only will we blow up ships, but we will destroy the energy infrastructure of our neighbors and the entire region.' Just think about that," Rubio said. "Because I think that we skip over that like that's some sort of normal behavior. That's not normal behavior, but we are there to help protect against it."
Iran targeted U.S. air defenses then hit aircraft and buildings on Mideast bases, AP analysis finds

Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage, according to an Associated Press analysis.

The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The AP found that Iran initially focused its attacks on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, clearing the way for further strikes on warehouses, troop housing and more.

The damage has significantly reshaped the American foothold in the Middle East, with two regional officials saying the U.S. has moved many of its assets out of the Persian Gulf. That includes aircraft, air defense systems, communications systems and other equipment crucial to base operations, one of those officials said.

Most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, while U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted, the analysis of satellite imagery shows.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area.

Camp Buehring, also in Kuwait, faced even heavier losses. While Iranian attacks made most of its hangars inoperable, gathering places for troops sustained much more damage because the base had limited aircraft. Its gym was destroyed in March and a store for troops to buy products on the base was hit in late July.
Iran has no plans for talks with U.S., foreign minister says
Iran's top diplomat on Saturday said there were no plans to hold talks with the United States despite growing concerns over a return to war.

"Currently, there are no plans for meetings with American officials, and any speculation to the contrary is merely media assumption," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
"We see no need to meet with the Americans at present, our conditions are clear, and the mediators continue their consultations regarding them," Araghchi told Al Jazeera.

Qatari and Pakistani mediators met in Doha, Qatar, on Saturday, where an Iranian delegation was present. Iranian officials, through the Qatari mediators, received an outline for a peace deal from the U.S. last weekend, spearheaded by Vice President JD Vance.

"The American side's attempt to open the door to broader dialogue and understanding is considered a positive step, and if Washington's goal from Vance's message is to stir up differences, it will be a new mistake added to its previous errors," Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Regional leaders call for calm amid fears of new military escalation in Iran

Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs said on Saturday the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace. Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Waleed ElKhereiji told the audience that efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement to end the crisis with Iran.

"If you look at … the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region," he said. But he said no one can predict the outcome of the efforts.

Concerns are rising about a return to all-out war, especially after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S. President Trump has opined during recent rallies that he could quickly bring the war to an end through military action.
Speaking at the same event, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
"We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere," he said.
AP/CBS
Iran's supreme leader warns U.S. against resuming attacks
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, on Saturday warned the United States against launching fresh attacks, amid weeks of heightened tensions and repeated threats.

"If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them," said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his Telegram channel.

The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.
Khamenei has not been seen publicly since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei's killing in U.S.-Israeli strikes at the start of the war in February.
According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that "any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response."
CBS/AFP
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted "hostile drone" in Riyadh region
Saudi air defences intercepted a drone in the Riyadh region on Saturday, according to the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis.

"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone in the Riyadh region," Turki al-Malki wrote on X, adding that "debris from the interception fell without causing injuries." Malki did not say who launched the drone.

In recent weeks, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on Riyadh airport that forced its closure for two weeks and the cancellation of flagship events.
On Friday, Malki said the Houthis had targeted the Medina region, home to Islam's second holiest city, but the group later denied the claim.

The Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, airports and ships come after hostilities resumed in Yemen over the summer between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Riyadh.
More than 1,600 people have been killed and over 275,000 displaced since the fighting reignited, according to United Nations figures.
CBS/AFP
Supertanker caught fire after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Friday that a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil struck a naval mine and caught fire while using an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. The Guard said it was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after attempting to use unauthorized routes through the strait.

Iran has repeatedly warned vessels against passing through the strait without Tehran's permission. It has claimed responsibility for attacks on ships and said last month that vessels attempting to pass through the strait without authorization would face "destruction." Tehran has asserted control over much of the waterway since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

Earlier on Friday, the Guard's navy said three other tankers caught fire after striking mines in the strait, Iranian state TV reported. It claimed the vessels had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and ignored repeated radio warnings. Iran's report did not identify the vessels or provide details about the crews. The Associated Press could not verify those claims.

Meanwhile, Oman said it had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged tanker that was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, catching fire. It is unclear whether that incident is related to the fires described by Iran.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center also reported Friday that a vessel was struck by an "unknown projectile" south of Lavan, an island just off mainland Iran near Shidvar. The organization, part of the British military that monitors maritime safety, said the crew was safe.
Strikes blamed on Houthis target Yemen presidential palace

Yemen's Houthis targeted the presidential palace in Aden on Friday with two missiles, a police official told AFP, hours after Saudi forces said they had intercepted an attack by the group on the Gulf kingdom.
Aden, the seat of Yemen's Saudi-backed and internationally recognized government, has been targeted repeatedly since Yemen's dormant civil war reignited in July.

Two eyewitnesses told AFP they saw ambulances entering the palace in Aden, a large compound made up of several buildings including facilities used by government and Saudi-led coalition forces, after the incident.
Shortly before, residents and an AFP journalist said they heard two blasts in the city.
The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa to the north, most recently struck the perimeter of Aden's airport on Wednesday after saying they had targeted a naval base and a military camp last week.
October marks record high for reported strikes in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says

There were more strikes reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz than any other month during the Iran-U.S. war, according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre, which is supported by the Royal Navy.

There were just over 30 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman or Persian Gulf reported in October, with only March, the first month of the war, reporting even 30 attacks, according to the UKMTO. There were twice as many attacks in October as there were in September. While there were likely more attacks in the month, the UKMTO only counts attacks reported by verified vessels in the region.

The war also crossed the eight-month mark this week as it started on Feb. 28. Since the war started, there have been 145 reported incidents, the UKMTO said. While the UKMTO does not track who fired the projectiles that hit vessels, the vast majority of strikes came via Iran. Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps often claims responsibility for the attacks.
Iran has started to claim a large number of ships hitting mines in the region as well, though they largely do not appear on the list of incidents from the UKMTO.

Since July 6, 59 of the 81 projectile strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz region came along the southern route, the UKMTO said. The U.S. has championed the southern route, and used it to escort oil tankers out of the Persian Gulf, while Iran calls the route illegal and says ships need to travel north, along the Iranian coast.
Rubio hosts G20 ministers as Iran, Ukraine wars divide members

Secretary of State Marco Rubio opened talks Friday with G20 counterparts including Russia's Sergei Lavrov, in meetings set to be fractious as wars in Ukraine and Iran, alongside surging energy costs, fan discord.
The foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta takes place just days before crucial midterm elections, setting the stage for a December G20 leaders' summit in Miami at President Trump's Doral resort.
But ongoing conflicts have deepened rifts even as the United States seeks to focus on economic growth, trade imbalances and supply chain challenges in areas like energy and critical minerals.
Rubio warned at an opening plenary session that the world faces "interconnected economic and geopolitical crises, many of which pose severe threats" to the global economy.
He urged the G20 to work together against threats including strains to global energy and food supply chains, and on freedom of navigation.

Still, few breakthroughs are expected this week from the Group of 20 economies — which include China, India, Russia, Japan, Germany and France — as officials face divisions over Moscow's war on Ukraine and fallout from the conflict with Iran.
Global energy prices have rocketed since U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran from late February triggered Tehran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

"This is the last test case the G20 has, at least under the US G20 presidency, until Miami," Alisha Chhangani of the Atlantic Council told AFP. Its outcomes will affect how the December summit shapes up.
UAE says oil spill from tanker in Strait of Hormuz has been contained

No new oil leakage has been detected from the tanker GEM NO. 2 following an in the United Arab Emirates' territorial waters, as cleanup operations continue along the UAE coastline, the Persian Gulf nation's official WAM news agency reported.

WAM quoted the Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure as saying Friday that technical teams had repaired damaged parts of the vessel, restored some operating systems and assessed the ship's structural integrity. Authorities said the source of the spill had been stopped.
According to the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, the oil slick is concentrated off Umm Al-Quwain, extending toward coastal areas of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah.
Pollution levels have declined, while monitoring and cleanup operations continue.

The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. It did not assign blame, but Iran has repeatedly targeted commercial ships in and around the southern Strait of Hormuz, which includes the UAE coastline.
Saudis intercept drone, missile allegedly launched by Houthis
The Saudis intercepted a drone near the capital of Riyadh on Friday afternoon as well as a ballistic missile in southern Saudi Arabia, according to the country's Coalition Joint Forces Command.
The coalition said both were fired by the Houthis. It's unclear exactly where the missile was intercepted in southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have regularly targeted locations in Saudi Arabia, everywhere from just over the border from Yemen to hundreds of miles into the interior, including Riyadh. Airports have been a consistent target of Houthi attacks.
The Saudi coalition had earlier announced it intercepted a drone near the holy city of Mecca, which the Houthis denied was fired by their forces.
Lebanon charges 13 people over seized shipment of Hezbollah explosives

A Lebanese military court on Friday charged 13 people for their alleged involvement in shipping explosives to Hezbollah, a judicial source told the AFP news agency, after authorities seized the roughly 1,100-pound cargo earlier this month.

The charges come as pressure mounts on Hezbollah, long a major political and paramilitary force in Lebanon that the U.S. and Israel consider an Iran-backed terrorist organization. The group has been weakened by back-to-back wars with Israel and is now facing a concerted push from authorities in Beirut, with backing from the Trump administration, to disarm its military wing.
Only two of the 13 people charged over the explosives shipment have been detained, and only eight have been identified, with the remaining five known only by noms de guerre.

Proceedings have been opened "against 12 members of Hezbollah, and one of their spouses," a judicial official told AFP. They were charged with "violating government decisions, possession of arms and explosives, and criminal conspiracy to undermine the authority of the state," the source said.
In a rare admission, Hezbollah acknowledged ownership of the vehicle and its cargo, and even demanded the shipment be returned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has vowed that authorities "will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness."

In June, Lebanon and Israel that included the disarmament of Hezbollah and a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied territory in southern Lebanon, with the Lebanese army stepping in to secure the area.

So far, Hezbollah has flatly refused to disarm or acknowledge the ceasefire, and very little of what Israel calls its occupied "security zone" in southern Lebanon has been handed over to Lebanese forces.
CBS/AFP
Oman evacuates 25 crew members from vessels burning off its Strait of Hormuz coast
Oman's navy has evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel after it was targeted and a fire broke out on board, the Omani Maritime Security Center said in a statement Friday.

The evacuation was carried out in coordination with the Maritime Security Center approximately 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam Governorate, the northern tip of Oman that juts out into the center of the Strait of Hormuz.
Crew members were "provided with the necessary medical care," the navy said in a statement.

Earlier Friday, Iran's navy and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two ships were on fire after striking sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz after attempting to use shipping lanes close to Oman's coast that the U.S. military insists are safe and open, but Tehran considers illegal.
ExxonMobil profits double to $15.4 billion on oil price surge

Major U.S. oil and gas giant ExxonMobil reported Friday that its third-quarter profits had more than doubled to $15.4 billion, as it benefited from higher oil prices and refining margins due to the U.S.-Iran war.
Profits in the period were slightly more than double the $7.5 billion in the year-ago period.
Oil prices have been high since the start of the war. As of Friday, the two main benchmark products, Brent crude and U.S. West Texas Intermediate, remained up about 70% compared to a year ago.
CBS/AFP
Iranian navy claims "enemy drone" destroyed, 2 oil tankers on fire in Hormuz strait
The Iranian navy said Friday that an enemy drone was "struck and destroyed" east of the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement, the navy also said two oil tankers "were damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines," accusing the vessels of ignoring warnings and navigating in prohibited and unsafe waters with their tracking systems switched off.
It was not immediately clear if the two vessels referred to by the Iranian navy were the same tankers that Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps in the strait.
President Trump says Iran war "going to get wrapped up soon"
President Donald Trump said Friday that the war with Iran is "going to get wrapped up soon."
Speaking to Kansas City radio station KCMO ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the president said "it's going to get wrapped up soon," without specifying how.
"We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon," he added.
U.S. CENTCOM chief renews insistence that Iran's navy is destroyed and Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes are open

The commander of the U.S. military's Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, reiterated his longstanding assertions on Friday that Iran's navy is "at the bottom of the sea" and that southern commercial shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz are clear of Iranian mines and safe to navigate.

In a video posted on social media, Cooper said the U.S. had helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer, while the U.S. naval blockade had prevented Iran from exporting any oil through the strait.
Cooper said he had recently flown over the strait and seen U.S. military "assets in the air and on the water."

"What I didn't see," said Cooper, was Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps "out there at all. They patrolled the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters for decades, harassing and threatening and seizing commercial vessels at will, but they were not out there because Iran's navy is all at the bottom of the sea."

Cooper renewed the claim made by President Trump and the Pentagon since late August that "we also successfully cleared the strait's internationally recognized primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines. And today, U.S. forces remain highly vigilant and present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."

His comments came a day after Iran's navy claimed four vessels had struck sea mines and been disabled as the attempted to transit the strait via the U.S.-backed southern route. The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening, meanwhile, that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the strait.
It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines.
Source confirms to CBS News Qatari mediators are in Iran to convey tweaks to latest peace proposal
A source familiar with the ongoing diplomacy confirmed to CBS News that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday to convey the latest edits to a draft proposal to end the U.S. war with Iran.
The source said there were indications of progress being made.

A draft was presented by Qatari mediators last Sunday, and a response from Iran is expected by the weekend. The aim of the proposal is to avert a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which President Trump has threatened multiple times in recent weeks.
Iran says 2 tankers on "unauthorized route" in Strait of Hormuz had "incidents and were brought to a halt"

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.

The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.

The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
CBS/AFP
Qatari officials return to Iran to push for peace deal with U.S.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency, along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.

The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.

An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had , and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
U.S. military death toll since start of Iran war rises to 23, Pentagon says

The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.

Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.

Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.

The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations, which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
Saudi coalition says Houthi drone intercepted in Mecca region
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reported.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
CBS/AFP
Tanker struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz, U.K. navy says, as Iran claims four ships hit sea mines

A tanker was struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center reported, after Iran's navy claimed four ships had struck sea mines in the area.
UKMTO said the ship hit by a projectile was exiting the strait along the southern route, which the U.S. has encouraged international shipping companies to use, when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," UKMTO said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its military claimed in two separate announcements earlier Thursday that four tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires.

It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been struck by a projectile was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report from the maritime monitor suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Iran has not yet responded to letter from Vance, Iranian media says

Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.

Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.

body: Avalon Hill's deluxe rerelease of the classic dungeon crawl board game HeroQuest is getting a digital edition courtesy of Nomad Games, who previously adapted board games like Talisman, Love Letter, and Fury of Dracula. Expect goblin-bashing, trap-disarming, treasure-hunting, and spell-casting. I'll use my broadsword.

As well as solo play, with the computer taking on the role of the Evil Wizard and his minions, it'll support online multiplayer with up to four players as the heroes, and a fifth optionally taking over as the villainous Zargon. (It's based on the American version, so no Morcar here.)

The most promising detail revealed so far is the inclusion of a quest editor so players can create their own maps and missions, as well as downloading quests made by others through mod.io integration.

Hopefully it includes the rules additions from HeroQuest First Light, especially the option to just move eight squares per turn instead of rolling to move if there aren't any monsters on the board. Slogging across the dungeon to get back to the exit 2d6 squares at a time is a real chore otherwise.
