articles.headline: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto hack
keyFacts: Binance customers withdrew a net $3.64 billion in assets as the cryptocurrency exchange reopened on Sunday following a record hack.
The FBI and other major organisations have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack that impacted $6.3 billion in assets.
Binance stated it has covered roughly 95% of the stolen assets and will fully cover all losses linked to the incident.
body: - Published
Binance customers withdrew $3.64bn (Â£2.72bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following a record hack last week.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack, which is said to be the largest hack in history.

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, but that the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.

"Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," Binance posted on X.
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.34bn in funds, to deal with âthe fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.

Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

articles.headline: Zach Cregger Was 'Frustrated' the Conversation Around Resident Evil 'Didn't Have Anything to Do With the Movie'
keyFacts: Filmmaker Zach Cregger stated on a podcast that he was frustrated by fan discussions surrounding his Resident Evil film focusing on lore rather than the movie itself.
Despite pre-release backlash from fans over creative liberties, the Resident Evil film became a commercial success, grossing over $400 million globally.
Cregger suggested he is unlikely to direct future franchise films, though he left open the possibility and is currently working on an original sci-fi thriller titled The Flood.
body: Horror filmmaker Zach Cregger has explained why he was "frustrated" that much of the conversation around his Resident Evil film "didn't have anything to do with the movie."

The mind behind hits like Barbarian and Weapons touched on his feelings about the lead-up to the premiere of his latest project during an appearance on The Town with Matthew Belloni podcast. Anyone who paid a second of attention to the Resident Evil movie adaptation knows Cregger struggled to win fans over ahead of its release, and it's something that left him frustrated from a number of angles.

"I think I was frustrated at the conversation around Resident Evil and how much of the conversation really didn't have anything to do with the movie," he said when explaining why he will likely stray from making movies based on established IP in the future.

"It had everything to do with whether the movie was living up to the different standards that different fans of the games had. Whether it was using the characters or not, or what did I get wrong in the lore? It was just a lot about, 'Why isn't this like the source material, or why is it good that it's not like the source material? All the conversation just felt like it was about not the movie."

Skeptical viewers harped on most of the same topics between the release of Resident Evil's first trailer and its theatrical premiere. Where's Leon? Why is it snowing in Raccoon City? Why does Austin Abrams' character have a smartphone? This vocal group of fans spent most of their time worried about what the film meant for the games it was based on and less about how it might carve out its own place in Capcom's wider universe.

Although Cregger did his best to explain that he took creative liberties to improve the overall quality of the movie, he did little to calm the storm of those who have longed to see the faces and places they know and love on the big screen. He did eventually go on to admit he was naïve to assume there would be any other outcome, but uncertain fans remained uneasy about what the final product might look like all the way up until its September 18 release date.
So, how did it do? Despite the backlash, it was a tremendous hit, and it's one Cregger is proud of.

The average movie fan who went to see Resident Evil was generally happy with a new, snowy vision of Raccoon City, too. The film premiered to great reviews (IGN gave it an 8/10 ) and opened to a whopping $108 million at the worldwide box office.

With a reported budget of $75 million, that was already a solid start, but audiences also continued to show up for the movie in the weeks that followed. Now, as the Halloween weekend draws to a close, Resident Evil has managed to cross $400 million across the globe. That's probably enough success to convince Sony to bring Cregger back for a sequel, but it may be best to keep expectations on that front low for now.

"I'm proud of the movie. I really love the movie," Cregger elaborated during the podcast appearance. "I realize I should have known better going into it. I should have understood that was going to be the case, but for some reason, I was a little shocked."

Did Cregger say he had ideas for a Resident Evil 2? Yes . Did he say he wanted to step away from franchise films after this one came out? Also yes . Now that the dust is starting to settle after fans spent months upset about his vision for the series, he has suggested he's not terribly interested in carrying the weight of an existing IP. Still, for him, it's a "never say never" situation.

The conversation around Resident Evil may have given Cregger more than he bargained for, so we'll have to wait to see what happens next. In the meantime, he's tinkering away on his next original film, The Flood . A sci-fi thriller written, produced, and directed by Cregger, the movie will star Hunger Games veteran Jennifer Lawrence when it premieres August 11, 2028.
While we wait for updates, you can read about how the Resident Evil movie boosted sales for Capcom's game series . Be sure to also read up on how watchers reacted to the film's divisive ending .

articles.headline: Collins accuses Schumer of pushing attack ads filled with 'outright lies' in tight Maine race
keyFacts: Sen. Susan Collins accused Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democrats of running attack ads filled with outright lies in her tight Maine reelection race.
Collins stated during a Fox News interview that identical false ads were used against multiple Republican senators as part of a national strategy.
Collins and her Democratic rival Troy Jackson are tied at 49% in the latest poll ahead of Election Day.
body: Sen. Susan Collins on Sunday blasted Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Party over what she described as a wave of false attack ads targeting her and other Republican candidates, saying she has never seen a campaign with "so many outright lies."

She made the remarks during an interview with Fox News on Sunday, just two days before Election Day in Maine, where she is seeking reelection in a closely watched race against Democratic rival Troy Jackson. According to the latest Fox News poll, the two candidates are tied at 49%.
Collins accused Democrats of following "Chuck Schumer's playbook," pointing to attack ads she said were nearly identical to those targeting other Republican lawmakers.
MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

"One of the outrageous, completely false ads against me had to do with Jeffrey Epstein. And it turns out, in talking to two of my colleagues who are in tough races, that they had virtually identical ads run against them. So this is part of Chuck Schumer's playbook," she said.
"There are a lot of differences between my opponent and me, but I've never seen a campaign with so many outright lies. It's very frustrating," she added.
Collins further accused Democrats of trying to shift the focus away from local issues and toward divisive national political battles.
"It's certainly an attempt by my opponent and Chuck Schumer and their allies to nationalize this race," she said.
SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Turning to her own campaign, Collins portrayed herself as a bipartisan lawmaker willing to work across party lines, arguing that the Senate needs more centrists as moderates increasingly leave Washington.
"Unfortunately, a lot of them have given up and retired or decided they just didn't want to run again. And that's one reason I am running again," she said.
"We need more people who are willing to work across party lines. That is really important," she said.
FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE

She also described herself as the "most independent senator on either side of the aisle," pointing to her voting record and saying her decisions are based on what she believes is right, rather than who occupies the White House or what President Donald Trump supports.

"There's this phony figure out there that I voted with President Trump 95% of the time. That's based on a sample of only 30% of the votes. If you look at a broader sample of 90% of the vote, that drops significantly to like 72%. And I voted against the president's policies 138 times," she said.

While Jackson previously told Fox News that he believes he has a "good shot" at defeating Collins , the longtime Republican senator touted strong voter support and said she is more optimistic than ever about her reelection chances.
"I'm feeling very optimistic based on the great response I get in visiting communities all over the state," she said.

articles.headline: Anthropic wants to use Claude AI to help discover new lifesaving drugs, says 'the best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs'
keyFacts: Anthropic is expanding the use of its Claude AI across pharmaceutical research to help biotechnology developers accelerate the creation of new medicines.
Partner companies reported successes including shorter CAR T-cell components, rapid generation of antibody designs, and a reduction in manufacturing documentation review time.
Anthropic stated that working directly with drug developers helps identify weaknesses in its models and plans to extend its involvement through additional partnerships.
body: - Anthropic is expanding Claude's role across several stages of drug development
- Generate Biomedicines reports a 70% reduction in CAR T-cell component length
- Modified immune cells produced roughly ten times more cancer-detecting receptors
Anthropic is expanding Claude’s involvement in pharmaceutical research, working with biotechnology developers on projects intended to accelerate the creation of new medicines.
The AI company has laid out in a new blog post how it is examining scientific and administrative obstacles affecting drug development, from molecular design to clinical trial preparation.
Its collaborations involve potential treatments for cancer, food allergies and rare muscular disorders, although most of the treatments remain at experimental stages.
Claude enters drug development programmes
At Generate Biomedicines, six scientists used Claude Code to modify a component of CAR T-cell therapy, traditionally employed against blood cancers.
Their work sought to create additional room for genetic instructions that could help the treatment address solid tumours.
The redesigned component was approximately 70% shorter, while laboratory experiments found that immune cells produced roughly ten times more receptors.
The modified cells also destroyed cancer cells more effectively and maintained their activity for longer periods, according to the reported findings.

Divergence Labs used Claude to develop antibody candidates for a potential food-allergy treatment involving the immune molecule IgE.
The system generated approximately 35,000 molecular designs within one month, producing potential molecules for both functions required by the proposed treatment.
Initial experiments identified three designs capable of binding to IgE and another 20 capable of detaching it from immune cells.
Three of the 20 designs appeared more effective than the standard medication at removing IgE from immune cells.
BigHat Biosciences combined Claude with automated laboratory equipment to improve two antibody fragments being considered for future medicines.
Researchers manufactured and tested approximately 1,010 variations over ten weeks, examining binding strength, stability and unwanted molecular aggregation.
The strongest cancer-targeting version bound its intended target more than 10 times as tightly and retained stability at temperatures 18°C higher than the original.
The other fragment, intended for longer-lasting medicines, aggregated more than 100 times more slowly than its original version.
Enveda applied Claude to manufacturing documentation, which had consumed up to 75% of some chemists’ working time.
During an assessment spanning 1,061 pages, the system identified all 11 problems previously discovered by human reviewers, as well as seven additional issues.
The approach reduced manual checking time by 89%, bringing the review process from more than 25 hours to under three.
Anthropic expands into clinical research and drug creation
Anthropic has also partnered with Bristol Myers Squibb to assess clinical study plans and estimate their chances of success.
Michael Pourdehnad, the pharmaceutical company's senior vice president for early clinical development, said: “From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis.”
He explained that this helped evaluate development options that would otherwise have required several days of work.
The companies intend to extend their collaboration further, examining Claude’s potential contribution to decisions during early clinical development.
Anthropic says working directly with drug developers helps identify weaknesses in its models and opportunities for improvement across scientific research.
The company also intends to extend Claude's involvement through additional partnerships, research programmes and tools for life-science organizations.

articles.headline: How Antonelli 'blew everyone away' to make Formula 1 history
keyFacts: Formula 1 driver Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in the history of the sport.
Fellow drivers Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen, and Lando Norris praised Antonelli for his exceptional skill and consistency throughout the season.
Antonelli stated that overcoming the difficulties and high pressure of his shaky debut season last year helped him mature as a driver.
body: - Published
Just after Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were united in their assessment of his achievement.
"Incredible," they both said. Coming from the two most successful champions on the current grid, the men who are first and third in the all-time list of F1 record-holders, it meant something.
That Antonelli shared the Mexico City Grand Prix podium with these two titans meant something, too.

To Antonelli, firstly, who said: "I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it's just an incredible moment. And as well to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special and a moment that will live and will always be remembered."
So, too, though, for its symbolism. Antonelli seems destined to join them among the list of all-time greats of the sport, judging by the scale of his achievement this year.
"There are going to be others," said 1996 world champion Damon Hill, commentating for BBC Radio 5 live.
"I don't see anything else other than him getting better and better. He's going to have to go through hard times as well, but no one is going to doubt his incredible talent."
No one indeed. Not any more, anyway.

Antonelli's first title comes at the end of only his second season in F1. When he was drafted into Mercedes last year - to replace Hamilton, no less - there were those who said he was too inexperienced.

For some of last year, he looked it. There were flashes of promise, but by and large it was a shaky debut season, one that did not live up to Antonelli's billing as potentially the next generational talent.
So when it became clear that Mercedes would start this season with the best car, it was his team-mate George Russell, who had comfortably beaten him in 2025, who was favourite for the championship.
But that was without reckoning on the remarkable step forward Antonelli made in his development over last winter.

He finished the first race on Russell's tail. He took his maiden victory in the second, the first of five consecutive wins with which he took control of the championship. Since then, he has never looked like losing it.
Even when Mercedes' early season advantage was wiped out by their rivals, Antonelli was always there, always a factor. Which is more than can be said for Russell.

In that sense, it is important to see his achievement in context. Had the comparative performance between Russell and Antonelli carried on as it did last year, this championship may well have had a different complexion.

It could have been a season during which Russell and Hamilton were neck and neck in the title fight for most of the year - indeed, Russell has now slipped behind both Verstappen and Hamilton in the points table.
Instead, it has been a story of one driver's domination. His performances have been so strong that he has removed pretty much all jeopardy from the title fight.
That has not made it the most exciting season to watch, but it speaks volumes for the level at which Antonelli has performed. All because of the progress he has made - and his remarkable consistency.

"At his age," said Verstappen, "to be so solid, not make big mistakes, and of course also beat your experienced team-mate, he's just driven incredible, and I'm very proud of him, how he has handled himself this whole season."
Lando Norris, the outgoing world champion, was also effusive in his praise.
"It couldn't have gone to a better person," he said. "He's a genuine guy, very, very kind, and he has driven unbelievably well this year, better that what everyone was expecting of him.
"He's certainly not had an easy season in terms of his competition being incredibly high. He has gone up against the best drivers in the world, all in very good cars, and he's blown everyone away.

"I hope everyone gives him enough credit for what he's achieved this year. He's made everyone else look silly. He's driven that well and he's been able to click with his car, he's worked hard to understand how to drive this car and he's exploited it better than anyone else.
"So he should be very proud. He has achieved history and I am very, very happy for him."
For Antonelli, the difficulties of last year were formative, and critical in what he has been able to achieve this.

"The fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to F1," he said, "or I wasn't ready for it - which at some point last year I probably looked like I wasn't - being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year.
"Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver, as a person.
"Still this year I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better, so it's just a constant learning process.
"Last year being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."
One of those moments was this weekend.
He admitted after qualifying that he had been "tight", not driving as well as he could have, a result of the pressure of the moment.

"Austin, I was much more aggressive, much more present in the moment," said Antonelli, "while in Mexico, yesterday in qualifying, I was a bit more tense in a way because I also wasn't as intense in the way I was driving.
"So definitely, it hasn't been easy on that side. But now finally, we clinched it and now we can just enjoy the rest of the season."
The potency of the moment was clear to see after the race.
Antonelli admitted he was so emotional on the last lap as he followed Verstappen and Hamilton home that he was struggling to see.
"I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying basically and I couldn't see clearly ahead," he said. "I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.
"It was very special and a lot of memories went through my mind in that moment."
Then his father Marco and mother Veronica, who have been so important in his rise to F1, were there to greet him at the end.
Marco has been virtually ever-present this season, providing quiet support for his son whenever needed.

"To have my dad during the whole season was very important," said Antonelli, "because, first of all, he was the one keeping me grounded, especially after very high moments, but as well he was the one that was always there when I was facing a difficult situation or I wasn't feeling the best ahead of a session."
Then, in the champions' news conference, he became so emotional at one point as he remembered his late grandfather that he could not talk, and had to take a minute to compose himself.
"Oh my god," he said, after he had collected himself. "I cried way too much today. But it's good."

articles.headline: How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
keyFacts: Apple does not guarantee how many updates will be available for tvOS or how long streaming boxes will be supported.
Older Apple TV models have historically received major software updates for eight to ten years.
The new Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13 for $299 with an A19 chip.
body: How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
Older Apple TVs have received up to a decade of updates, but Apple doesn't promise that.

At $299, the new Apple TV 4K is a lot to pay for a little black box that sits under your TV waiting for you to pick a show to watch. The fourth-generation model will be available November 13 with an A19 chip, an improved Siri Remote and hands-free Siri controls. For that price, how many years can you expect it to last before the next upgrade beckons?

Apple doesn't guarantee how many updates will be available for tvOS or how long its streaming boxes will be supported. But its history is a pretty good indication. Older Apple TVs have received major software updates for eight to 10 years, with security patches continuing beyond that. The hardware may continue to function long after it exits official support, with software and app compatibility concerns the most likely reasons for replacing one.
How long does Apple support an Apple TV for?

While the Apple TV HD was introduced in 2015, and the first Apple TV 4K in 2017, both were updated to tvOS 26 in 2025. Plus, security patches were provided in tvOS 26.6 in July 2026. That's about 10 years of major software updates for the HD and eight for the original 4K, plus some security support.

The impressive streak came to an end in September 2026 with tvOS 27. Apple's new tvOS compatibility list begins with the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021, which means the 2015 and 2017 models can't get the latest operating system. Apple has not yet confirmed whether those older boxes will get additional security patches. It's not a guarantee that the new Apple TV 4K will get 10 years of support. Apple hasn't provided an estimate of how many years of tvOS updates to expect, so the best indication is its track record.

In contrast, Amazon promises at least four years of security updates for Fire TV devices bought new directly from the company, or through the model's published support date (if later). That's not the same as a major OS upgrade, but at least Fire TV customers have a minimum support deadline in writing.
When should you actually replace your Apple TV?

Not being able to update to the latest version of tvOS doesn't make your Apple TV an expensive brick. Netflix still supports the Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K, even though neither is eligible for tvOS 27. That could change as developers raise their minimum software requirements, potentially leaving older devices unable to install or update certain apps.

A better way to think about your Apple TV is to consider its performance, not its age. When menus start to become painfully slow, apps begin to crash or a service that you care about stops working, an upgrade makes more sense. Security is also a factor, especially if your Apple TV is used as a smart home hub and no longer gets patched.

Upgrading is a tougher pill to swallow with the newest release costing $299. Apple's Siri AI beta will also be available on the second-generation Apple TV 4K and newer (if the Home admin has an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad), so you don't have to buy the latest box just for Siri AI. The 2026 Apple TV 4K does have some significant improvements over the 2022 version, such as a faster A19 processor and built-in microphones for hands-free control. But it's a significant amount to pay if you're already happy with your current Apple TV.

Then there's the Siri Remote, which frequently finds itself in the sofa. If yours is lost or breaks down, you can use your iPhone as a TV remote instead of replacing the whole setup. Apple's latest Siri Remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models and even the 2015 Apple TV HD, and a replacement costs $59.

articles.headline: Lions shaken after All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell taken to hospital with ‘scary’ neck injury
keyFacts: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury in the fourth quarter against the Minnesota Vikings and was taken to a local hospital.
Lions head coach Dan Campbell stated that Jack Campbell was breathing and alert when he left the field.
The Lions stated that Campbell would remain in the hospital overnight for continued evaluation and monitoring.
body: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was taken to a local hospital after being injured during the fourth quarter of his team’s 19-15 victory over the Minnesota Vikings.

“Thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said after the game. “He’s being taken care of. We don’t have any new information. We’ll keep you updated as this thing goes. But we are thinking about him. We are thinking about him.”
The Lions later said that Campbell would be kept in hospital overnight.

“Jack Campbell is resting and will remain in a local hospital tonight, for continued evaluation and monitoring,” the Lions said in a statement. “The team will provide further updates as we have them.”
Jack Campbell, a first-team All-Pro last season, was injured while tackling Vikings tight end TJ Hockenson in the fourth quarter.

The 26-year-old lay motionless facing the ground and was surrounded by medical personnel for nine minutes while being strapped to a board. He did not signal to the Ford Field crowd as he was driven off on a cart toward the tunnel.
“He’s breathing, he’s alert when he left,” Dan Campbell told the Lions Radio Network.
Lions quarterback Jared Goff was shaken up while observing the situation.

“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff said. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father. Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be alright. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that, it’s going to be him.”
Campbell, a fourth-year pro, was credited with three tackles prior to the injury. He has 57 this season after a career-high 176 last season. The Lions picked him in the first round of the 2023 draft.

articles.headline: Arsenal’s statement win over Liverpool is massive, it’s a one-horse title race
keyFacts: Arsenal defeated Liverpool 1-0 at Anfield with a goal from Kai Havertz, securing their first away league win against Liverpool since 2012.
Former defender Ashley Williams said the Premier League title race is effectively a one-horse race with Arsenal leading the competition.
The victory moved Arsenal three points clear at the top of the table with 24 points from their first nine matches.
body: Arsenal already have one hand on the Premier League title after beating Liverpool at Anfield.
That is according to former Premier League defender Ashley Williams , who believes the champions are effectively in a league of their own.
Arsenal have been told they are in a one-horse title race after beating Liverpool Getty
The Gunners moved three points clear of City after their 1-0 win over Liverpool .
Kai Havertz’s first half goal proved to be the winner as they secured their first Premier League victory at Anfield since 2012.
It leaves the Reds nine points adrift of Arsenal , whilst Brighton and Chelsea are both five points off the pace.
Meanwhile, the Seagulls are the only team to take points off of Mikel Arteta’s side , who have won eight of their nine matches to date.
Is the title race already over?
Williams does not expect Brighton to be able to keep in touch with the defending champions throughout the campaign, though.
Instead, he believes the title picture can already be considered a ‘one-horse race’.
Speaking on The Final Word, he admitted: “We’ve seen other teams win the league like Leicester but I don’t think Brighton can topple Arsenal this season.
“Before the season started I said it was a one-horse race and then I thought maybe it wasn’t but now I’m back to thinking it’s just Arsenal.”
Williams continued: “It feels like a bit of a statement win, doesn’t it?
“We’ve become accustomed to this; Arsenal get the job done.
The Gunners are three points clear at the top of the Premier League Getty
“Not to say that they weren’t good either, by the way. They were very good. They defended very well.
“They also created more chances but you’ve got to go there at places like Anfield and dig in. It’s hard to play at Anfield.
“I don’t care what team you are in the world. You go there, you dig in, you get your points, you get back on the bus happy. So, massive, massive win for Arsenal today.”
Arteta verdict on Arsenal win
Prior to Sunday’s victory, Arsenal had not won at Anfield in the Premier League since September 2012.
On that occasion, current manager Arteta was in the Gunners’ starting line-up as they came away 2-0 winners.
Reflecting on the importance of ending their Merseyside drought after the match, he said: “It’s been a long time, it’s been too long.
Arteta guided Arsenal to their first league win at Anfield since 2012 Getty
“So everybody attached to the football club should feel very, very proud because of the difficulty of the task that we had today.

“After getting out of the cup in the manner that we did and then being able to come here four days later and perform, compete and earn the right to win the game, tells you the story of of the beautiful game that we are involved in and how crazy and made it can drive you.
“That’s why I think it’s important to stay emotionally in control, otherwise it’s difficult to handle, but I’m extremely proud of what the boys have done.”
Arsenal set title pace
Arsenal’s latest win sees them earn 24 points after nine matches of the current campaign.
It marks the most by a team at this stage of a Premier League season since the Gunners achieved the same tally in 2022/23.
They have only amassed more points after nine matches on two previous occasions.
Arsenal have dropped just three points in their opening nine matches Getty
Those came during the 2004/05 and 2007/08 seasons, with Arsenal accumulating 25 points under Arsene Wenger on both occasions.
However, neither campaign ended in title glory as the Gunners instead finished second and third, respectively.

articles.headline: Gag Order is a co-op, SCP-ish horror shooter about surviving as best you can against some nasty, tentacle covered cephalopod creatures
keyFacts: Gag Order is a co-op horror shooter where players hunt and survive against tentacle-covered cephalopod creatures.
Players act as a research lab's Guardian Unit responding to a distress signal in a hostile complex.
The game is scheduled to be released by the end of 2026.
body: What makes Carrion interesting obviously lies in playing as the monster in a horror game rather than being the one chased down by it. The game's nasty tentacle monster still gives me the heebie jeebies, so I really would hate to be hunted by one. This is where I point you towards Gag Order, a shooter where you are in fact hunted by a disgusting cephalopod creature all while tracking down a distress signal.

Gag Order is not designed to be played solo, it feels wrong to call it friendslop given how unfriendly it is in vibes, but it does feel like it fits into a similar lineage as Lethal Company at the very least. In it, you are a research lab's Guardian Unit member, and you get a distress call "from one of the core parts of the complex." Upon arrival, the atmosphere is rotten, and you quickly come to understand that you are not equipped for what you have to deal with.

The solution, then, is to take care of those nightmare-inducing cephalopod creatures. Except during the first phase of a run, it sounds like they're invincible. Your guns do seem to be able to fend them off at the very least, but it's the second phase, which is geared around a "fast paced team-bossight" where it sounds like you'll be trying to take these things down. I'm not quite sure what the process is to get between those two phases, but I'm quite fond of the vibes on display.

It feels a touch reminiscent of 2000s shooters with some slightly contemporary mechanical sensibilities. I'm fond of the light SCP vibes it has going on, alongside the faint surrealness of certain elements like a bunch of crows hanging out in an abandoned office building. Creepy! Good looking stuff. Gag Order is apparently due out by the end of 2026, though we're obviously getting close there, so it's worth keeping an eye on it by throwing it a wishlist on Steam, if it takes your fancy.

articles.headline: Patrick Stewart, Our Captain Of Multimedia CD-ROM Edutainment
keyFacts: Actor Patrick Stewart narrated 1990s multimedia CD-ROM educational software such as Nine Worlds and Compton's Interactive Encyclopedia.
The 1997 educational software Nine Worlds allowed users to explore the solar system with audio narration provided by Stewart.
Stewart's prominent voice and roles in projects like Star Trek helped establish him as an educational guide during the early era of CD-ROM computers.
body: In 1997, Patrick Stewart took me on a voyage through the stars from the comfort of the family computer room. An interactive expansion of a 1993 video cassette, Nine Worlds allowed you to travel the solar system, pick up gift shop postcards, scientific and cultural history of each neighboring planet, all accompanied by bombastic (and slightly compressed) renditions of Gustav Holstâs famous celestial suites. And of course, with the guided audio tour from Stewart himself, whose impassioned chronology of Mars only netted me a C+ on my homework.
“To the Romans and Greeks, it was the god of war,” orates computer Stewart, “to others IT WAS THE RED EYE OF THE DEVIL HIMSELF!”

In the days since his shocking passing, fans have found themselves with so much to parse from the multifaceted thespian. Of course, to most, he was the eloquent, insightful Captain Jean-Luc Picard, whose fascinations of the cosmos led the crew on Star Trek: The Next Generation. To others he was the fatherly Professor X across the sprawling X-Men films. He was also a master of stagecraft, an outspoken advocate, a baker of erotic cakes, and a Beavis and Butt-Head superfan.

To those of a certain age, he was also an educator. Or, more specifically, an edutainer. Following Mystâs bank-making showcase of what CD-ROMs were capable of, classrooms and home computers experienced a surge of educational software. There had long existed Math Blasters and illustrious typing teachers, but with the assistance of compressed video and tinny audio, publishers sought to bring the classroom experience home.

While most celebrities needed to be charged on a DUI to edutain, the Next Gen crew seemed eager to moonlight as teachers. Of course, LeVar Burton had long hosted Reading Rainbow by the time he donned La Forgeâs visor, setting some precedent. While Riker was elsewhere teaching celebrity poker, Patrick Stewart captained numerous suites of multimedia CD-ROMs.

Sure, narrating a cultural history of our solar system makes sense given his resume, but Stewart was also recruited to guide young users in Compton’s Interactive Encyclopedia, a literary play-by-play of the Titanicâs final hours, among many other loose discs. His outstanding voice, powerful but kind, made him an ideal messenger for worldly information. It was an era where people were still learning how to use these machines, never mind learn from them. And in this brief era of scholarly CD, Stewart passed on the fascinations exhibited by his most famed performances.

While it didnât do me a ton of good on my immediate school work, many of these pieces of software imparted some deeply rooted pieces of information, continuing to rattle around my skull. As someone who would later on adore passing out to Carl Sagan, I didnât fully appreciate the psychic history of the Red Planet offered by Stewart. But the amount of context and culture squished into a meager disc is a fascination of its own. Where and how kids learn from computers going forward might be dubious, but there was an era of enthusiasm to reimagining games and education. When we aspired to reach higher, Stewart found himself a star there too.

articles.headline: This legendary board game could take decades to complete
keyFacts: Andy Taeger and James Purcell are attempting to become the first people to complete the notoriously complex board game Campaign for North Africa.
The participants stated that the game tracks extreme details, such as calculating water evaporation and the extra water Italian infantry need to boil pasta.
The pair estimated that playing the game will realistically take between 20 and 30 years to complete.
body: This legendary board game could take decades to complete
Andy Taeger & James Purcell are trying to become the first people ever complete the board game Campaign for North Africa. The is so complex it could take decades to finish.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

In the U.K., two friends have begun a challenge that many people believe is impossible. The board game Campaign for North Africa is legendary for its complexity and detail and its extreme time commitment. Andy Taeger and James Purcell are trying to become the first people ever to complete it. Hi to both of you.
JAMES PURCELL: Hi. It's James here.
ANDY TAEGER: Andy here. Hello.

PFEIFFER: So this board game covers a period of World War II that lasted roughly three years. Yet the game itself could take almost 10 times that, you know, many years more. What is it that makes it what you guys have described as comically complicated?

PURCELL: I suppose, first and foremost, we aren't generals. So we have no experience in warfare. There is everything to keep track of in this game down to how much water each unit has to drink, how much of that water evaporates, just about every granular detail you can think of.
PFEIFFER: (Laughter).
TAEGER: There's a rule Italian infantry uses more water so they could boil their pasta.
PFEIFFER: The pasta is that the Italians are going to go through drinking water faster, and they need to calculate that in?
PURCELL: Yeah. Apparently, they have to use more to boil their pasta. I'm not sure how accurate that is, but that's part of the rules.
PFEIFFER: All right, so the big question is - why? Why are the two of you doing this, if you know it could take years or even decades to complete?
PURCELL: We'd love to give an answer that makes some aspect of sense, but we really don't know why we're doing this.
PFEIFFER: (Laughter).

PURCELL: We heard about the game from a friend in passing. A few weeks later, me and Andy realized that we've been thinking about the game, and we thought, we may as well give it a try. We had no reason to think we could, and even now, two years into preparation, we still don't really know that we have any claim that we can do it. But we're going to try.

PFEIFFER: You just mentioned your two years of prep. You've created this companion podcast called "War With A Mate." I think it has about 100 episodes so far. The first 14 episodes are just about the rules. Do you think that by the time you actually start playing the game, it will still seem fun and interesting after all the practice?

TAEGER: I hope so, at least getting back into it 'cause we, yeah, finished our practice run. We're just about to start the main game. So we've got that excitement going in at the minute, but we'll see how long that holds before it turns to regret.

PFEIFFER: To do this kind of commitment means your friendship is going to have to stay strong, and you're going to be with each other a lot playing this game. How do you think your friendship will fare as you start doing this and know that if the friendship doesn't survive, you can't finish the game?

PURCELL: Andy and I used to be housemates for about three years, so we've spent a lot of time around each other previously, and our thinking is, if we've managed to live together, surely we can play a board game for 20 years together. That should be fine.
PFEIFFER: (Laughter).
PURCELL: But if the friendship suffers partway through, maybe we'll just have to play the game in silence.
PFEIFFER: What is your best estimate - when could you be done by?

TAEGER: Based on how fast we were going with our practice run that we wrapped up a few months ago, we - still be looking at about 15 to 20 years. We're going to add a bit onto that. We're realistically looking at somewhere between 20 and 30.
PFEIFFER: That is Andy Taeger and James Purcell. They are trying to be the first people to finish one of the world's most complicated games, which no one has finished before. Thank you.
PURCELL: Thank you.
TAEGER: Thank you.

articles.headline: At Dead of Night sequel The Great Hugo is coming "(very) soon"
keyFacts: Baggy Cat Games confirmed that the sequel At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo is coming very soon.
The sequel follows Maya five years after the original game as she investigates a Tudor manor house for answers.
The exact release date for the sequel has not yet been announced.
body: Baggy Cat Games, the team behind viral FMV horror game At Dead Of Night, has confirmed that a sequel is "coming (very) soon".
At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

At Dead Of Night became famous quickly during the pandemic thanks to streamers and content creators like Markiplier, 8-BitRyan, John Wolfe, and DomPlays, who introduced us to Jimmy Hall, a creepy hotel landlord hellbent on recruiting an audience for his late-night comedy show and psychopathic comedy alter ego, Hugo Punch.
The new game, subtitled The Great Hugo, picks up half a decade later.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."
Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

If you're still in the Halloween mood - and why wouldn't you be; horror games are for life, not just for Halloween - the developer of horror hit The Mortuary Assistant released Playable Archive this week as a Halloween freebie.

articles.headline: Can’t commit to vegetarianism but want animals to suffer less? You’ve got options.
keyFacts: A Vox advice column suggested people with health issues adopt a reducetarian diet to balance animal welfare with their personal well-being.
The column cited philosophical pragmatism, which advocates balancing multiple values instead of adhering to universal moral rules about eating animals.
To lower animal suffering, the article suggested buying pasture-raised meat, choosing certified humane products, or setting specific dietary parameters.
body: Editor’s note, November 1, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary . The one below was originally published in August 2025.

This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here .

I typically eat vegetarian, and have considered going fully vegan out of concern for animal welfare. But lately my on-again, off-again gastrointestinal problems have been acting up, and I’ve had to go back on a more restricted diet to manage my symptoms — no spice, no garlic or onions, nothing acidic, and nothing caffeinated. Sticking to a “bland” diet is hard enough, but doing so while vegetarian is very difficult when things like tomatoes and onions and grapefruits are off the table.

I know a lot of people with these issues eat fish or meat, and some medical professionals recommend drinking chicken bone broth to soothe flare-ups. I don’t want to abandon my commitment to animal welfare while my gut sorts itself out, but my food options are limited right now. How should I approach this?
Dear Would-Be Vegetarian,

You’re not alone in finding it hard to stick to a purely vegetarian diet. Only 5 percent of American adults say they’re vegetarian or vegan . What’s more, one study found that 84 percent of people who adopt those diets actually go back to eating meat at some point. And most of them aren’t even dealing with the gastrointestinal problems you face.

So, it speaks to the depth of your moral commitment that you’re really wrestling with this. I’ll have some concrete suggestions for you in a bit, but first I want to emphasize that how you approach the question of meat-eating will depend on your underlying moral theory.

There’s a classic split in moral philosophy between deontologists and utilitarians. A deontologist is someone who thinks an action is moral if it’s fulfilling a duty — and we have universal duties like, “always treat others as ends in themselves, never as means to an end.” From that perspective, killing an animal for food would be inherently morally wrong, because you’re treating the animal as a means to an end.

Meanwhile, a utilitarian is someone who thinks that an action is moral if it produces good consequences — and behaving morally means producing the most happiness or well-being possible, or reducing the most suffering possible. Utilitarian philosophers like Peter Singer argue that we should be reducing, and ideally eliminating, the suffering that animals endure at our hands.

Deontologists and utilitarians are often pitted against each other, but they actually have one big thing in common: They both believe in a universal moral principle — whether it’s “always treat others as ends in themselves” or “always maximize happiness.”

A lot of people find that comforting, because it offers certainty about how we should act. Even if acting morally requires hard sacrifices, it’s incredibly soothing to think, “If I just do X, then I’ll know for sure that I’m being a good person!”
But these moral theories assume that all the complexity of human life can be reduced to one tidy formula. Can it, really?
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!

Another school of philosophy — pragmatism — says we should be skeptical of fixed moral principles. Human life is so complicated, with many different factors at play in any ethical dilemma, so we should be pluralistic about what makes outcomes valuable instead of acting like the only thing that matters is maximizing a single value (say, happiness). And human society is always evolving, so a moral idea that makes sense in one context may no longer make sense in a different context. To a pragmatist, moral truths are contingent, not universal and unchanging.

I think one pragmatist who can really help you out is the University of Michigan’s Elizabeth Anderson. In a 2005 essay applying pragmatism to the question of eating meat , the philosopher points out that for most of human history, we couldn’t have survived and thrived without killing or exploiting animals for food, transportation, and energy. The social conditions for granting animals moral rights didn’t really exist on a mass scale until recently (although certain non-Western societies did ascribe moral worth to some animals).
“The possibility of moralizing our relations to animals (other than our pets),” Anderson writes, “has come to us only lately, and even then not to us all, and not with respect to all animal species.”

In other words, Anderson doesn’t think there’s some universal rule like “eating animals is inherently morally wrong.” It’s our social and technological circumstances that have made us more able than before to see animals as part of our moral circle . She also doesn’t believe there’s a single yardstick — like sentience or intelligence — by which we can judge how much of our moral concern an animal deserves. That’s because moral evaluation isn’t just about animals’ intrinsic capacities, but also about their relationships to us. It matters whether we’ve made them dependent on us by domesticating them, say, or whether they live independently in the wild .

It also matters whether they’re fundamentally hostile to us. Killing bedbugs? Totally fine! They may be sentient, but, Anderson writes, “We are in a permanent state of war with them, without possibility of negotiating for peace. To one-sidedly accommodate their interests…would amount to surrender.”
Anderson’s point is not that animals’ intelligence and sentience don’t matter. It’s that lots of other things matter, too, including our own ability to thrive.

With this pragmatic approach in mind, you can consider how to balance your concern for animal welfare with your concern for your own welfare. Instead of thinking in terms of a moral absolute that would force you into a “purist” diet no matter the cost to you, you can consider a “reducetarian” diet, which allows you to ease your own struggle while also taking care for animals seriously.
The key thing to realize is that some types of animal consumption cause a lot less suffering than others.

For one thing, if you’re eating meat, try to buy the pasture-raised kind and not the kind that comes from factory farms — the huge industrialized facilities that supply 99 percent of America’s meat . In these facilities, animals are tightly packed together and live under unbelievably harsh and unsanitary conditions. They’re also often mutilated without pain relief : think pigs being castrated, cows being dehorned, and hens being debeaked. Oh, and chickens have been bred to be so big that they’re in constant pain ; they live miserable lives from start to finish.

A pasture-raised label doesn’t mean an animal has been spared all of the harms of modern agriculture — it doesn’t guarantee that pain relief is used for painful procedures, and farm animals across different production systems have been bred to maximize production, which can take a toll on their welfare. And of course they’ll ultimately meet the same fate as those raised on factory farms — slaughter. But your goal here is to meaningfully reduce, not 100 percent eliminate, the harms. And at least pasture-raised animals have gotten to roam around in a field and engage in natural behaviors up until the end.

It’s a similar story for fish, by the way. More than half of the fish we eat comes from fish farms, which are basically just underwater factory farms. Wild-caught fish is not perfect — slow, suffocating deaths are common — but it’s better than farmed.

The caveat here is that a lot of the welfare labels you’ll see on animal products are basically a con . And some certification schemes have similar names, so you have to pay close attention. If you see the label “Certified Humane,” that’s genuinely higher-welfare — but don’t mistake it for “American Humane Certified,” which is really not. And be wary of putting much stock in labels like “cage-free” or “free-range.” They’re better than nothing, but because the terms are often ill-defined and unenforced, they’re not as meaningful as you might think. Here’s a good guide to separating the real deal from the advertising spin.

Another classic recommendation among animal welfare advocates is to eat bigger animals — in other words, go for beef rather than chicken. That’s both because of how miserable chickens’ lives are on factory farms and because, as my former colleague Kelsey Piper has written , it just takes way more chicken lives than cow lives to feed people. Cows are huge, producing about 500 pounds of beef apiece, while a chicken yields only a few pounds of meat. So, every year, the average American eats about 23 chickens and just over one-tenth of one cow .

That said, cows take a heavier toll on the climate than chickens do, so you don’t want to eat tons of beef either. The environment is also one of the key values at stake in our consumption choices, so that has to factor in, too.

Of course, another possibility — to the extent that this works with your gastrointestinal issues — is to reach for low-fiber plant-based foods like tofu, seitan, and the smorgasbord of newer products now available (like Beyond and Impossible burgers).

But assuming you’re going to eat meat, it’s a good idea to set some clear parameters and standards around your reducetarian diet. A lot of reducetarians — myself included — have fallen into the trap of saying, “I’ll reduce how much meat I eat,” but forgetting to quantify what that means. That can lead you to eat more meat than you’d intended. So it’s probably better to commit to something like “weekday vegetarian” or “vegan before six” — you can check out the Reducetarian Foundation for suggestions.

At the end of the day, remember that there’s a plurality of values at stake here, and no one of them necessarily trumps all the others. If you feel that eating some meat is important for your well-being right now, and you try to do that in ways that keep suffering for animals to a minimum, I don’t think you need to feel bad about that. That’s because you won’t be shirking your values: You’ll be recognizing that your values are plural, and you’re doing your best to balance between them. That may be the best any of us can really do.
Bonus: What I’m reading

The blogger Bentham’s Bulldog published a piece titled “ How to cause less suffering while eating animals .” It contains some of the same recommendations I mentioned above, but the underlying ethical framework is different and it makes one recommendation I didn’t: “offsetting” your meat consumption by donating to highly effective animal charities . I worry that offsetting might create a moral hazard, as with people offsetting their carbon emissions and then potentially feeling free to fly more. But it’s worth considering, particularly if you pair it with clear parameters around your reducetarian diet.

This Aeon essay answers a question I’ve often wondered about: Why haven’t other animals — say, birds — developed complex civilizations like we humans have? Why don’t they build rocket ships, argue about economic policy, and play canasta? I’m grateful to the evolutionary biologist who wrote this piece for finally giving me a satisfying answer.

I can’t stop thinking about this post on how AI companies may have designed chatbots to play an underspecified “helpful assistant” character who, due to being underspecified, looks to the internet for examples of how to play that role, finds tons of science fiction about cheesy robots, and thus starts to behave like a cheesy sci-fi robot (ChatGPT will say things like, “Gee, that really tickles my circuits!”). This post is mega-long, deeply trippy, and worth reading.

articles.headline: Trump Cabinet Secretary Torched For 'Disgusting' Racist Halloween Post
keyFacts: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins faced social media outrage Saturday over a Halloween post featuring a fake costume depicting a Black man as a SNAP fraudster.
Critics accused Rollins of promoting racist stereotypes reminiscent of past conservative welfare rhetoric used to justify cuts to government assistance programs.
Social media users also pointed out that President Donald Trump has pardoned or commuted the sentences of numerous individuals convicted of fraud.
body: A Halloween post from Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins sparked outrage on social media Saturday, with many accusing the Trump administration official of blatant racism.

“Some costumes come with a price tag. This one comes with a prison sentence. To anyone stealing from American taxpayers: The tricks are over. The treats are running out. Happy Halloween!” Rollins wrote on X alongside a fake Spirit Halloween costume depicting a Black man as a “SNAP Fraudster.”
Rollins’ post was likely a reference to the Trump administration’s attempts to root out so-called waste, fraud, and abuse within government social programs.

The depiction of a Black man as a “SNAP Fraudster” harkens back to many of the racist stereotypes conservative politicians have peddled for decades, going all the way back to President Ronald Reagan’s “welfare queen” rhetoric.
This rhetoric has frequently been used to justify cutting government assistance, as President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” did to SNAP benefits, Medicaid and a host of other programs.
Despite the Trump administration’s continued touting of its work to stop fraud, the president has pardoned or commuted the sentences of numerous individuals convicted of fraud.

articles.headline: November 2026 Skywatching Guide: Meteors, Planets, Stars and a Full Moon
keyFacts: All planets are visible during November, featuring an alignment of Mercury, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter between Nov. 14 and 25.
Three meteor showers peak in November, including the Southern Taurids, Northern Taurids, and Leonids.
The Beaver Moon supermoon peaks on Nov. 24, beginning a string of four consecutive supermoons that ends in 2027.
body: Autumn is marching right along, and so are the objects in the night sky. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time ending Nov. 1, the sun will set even earlier. That’ll give skygazers more time to see some cool sights without staying up horribly late or waking up unbearably early.
When to see each planet in November

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.
More from CNET

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, where it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.
Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.
Nov. 2-3: The moon, Mars and Jupiter dance party

The month begins with a meetup among Mars, Jupiter and the moon. The three will appear close together in the night sky, making them easy to spot: The moon is easy to find, and both planets are visible to the naked eye. On Nov. 2, the moon will be closer to Mars, and the trio will follow one another across the sky throughout the night. Regulus will also be in tow and readily visible to the naked eye.

Nov. 3 continues the good vibes. The moon slides over to the other side of Regulus on that night, but all four celestial bodies are still quite close together and easy to spot. Mars, Jupiter and Regulus will get even closer to each other as November progresses, but the moon moves even further away after Nov. 3.
Nov. 4-5: Southern Taurids meteor shower peaks

The Southern Taurids have technically been active since Sept. 20, and continue until Nov. 20. This long-running meteor shower peaks during the evening of Nov. 4 and morning of Nov. 5. It’s not a terribly strong meteor shower and should average about five meteors per hour. However, it often tosses bright fireballs, so what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.

The moon is 22% illuminated that night, which the American Meteor Society calls “favorable conditions” for viewing a meteor shower. You want to get as far away from light pollution as possible to give yourself even better odds, and make sure to dress for the weather. The Southern Taurids will appear to originate from the Taurus constellation, which rises in the east shortly after sunset and moves across the sky before setting in the west right before sunrise.
Nov. 9: The best night for hunting stars

It’s no secret that the full moon is usually the most popular celestial event to happen every month, but skygazers also value the new moon. This is because the moon is a significant source of light pollution, making many stars and planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, harder to see. With the new moon on Nov. 9, it’ll be the darkest night of November — and perfect for stargazing and night-sky photography.

Nov. 9 also happens to be Carl Sagan Day, an unofficial holiday to honor the visionary astronomer. If you’re stuck inside that night, you can always use the occasion to watch Sagan’s legendary Cosmos series, which is available for free on the Internet Archive or through various user uploads on YouTube.
Nov. 14-25: A four-planet alignment

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Nov. 14 there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Nov. 14 and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.
Nov. 11-12: Northern Taurids peaks

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 11 and the morning of Nov. 12. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Nov. 11, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.
Nov. 16-17: Leonids peaks

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It starts on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41%-illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.
Nov. 23-24: Supermoon

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.
Nov. 30: Another moon, Mars and Jupiter dance party

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.
All month: Constellations and asterisms

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object so you can find it.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

articles.headline: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
keyFacts: A new Science study shows that Manx shearwaters experience jet lag when they fly across time zones over the North Atlantic.
Researchers said that because these seabirds navigate using the Sun, their jet lag skews their internal compass.
Patrick Lewin and other researchers explained that effective solar navigation requires an internal clock, but the birds' clock is imperfect.
body: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it’s the middle of the night while the clock says it’s lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.
Clockwork compass

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

From there, they head out to feed anywhere from a few dozen to more than 1,000 kilometers into the Atlantic. To get back, shearwaters are thought to work out where they are located using a map sense, possibly based on smells, and then use the Sun as a compass to set their direction.

The trouble with navigating by the Sun, though, is that it moves across the sky. “You can imagine an animal or a human that wants to travel south all day. At sunrise, when the Sun’s in the east, it needs to be traveling 90 degrees clockwise of the Sun, but by midday it needs to be traveling straight towards the Sun, and by sunset it needs to be traveling 90 degrees anticlockwise of the Sun,” Lewin said. Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is. Birds, like nearly all animals, have such a clock built in. But the clock in Manx shearwaters is not perfect.
